claim: Liver trNK cells do not clearly express CD127 compared to thymic NK cells.
source: However, as compared to thymic NK cells, liver trNK (CD49a+ DX5−) cells did not clearly express the prototypic thymic NK cell marker, CD127 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A comparing CD127 expression levels.

claim: Liver trNK cells are present in athymic nude mice (Foxn1−/−).
source: To more definitively determine the relationship between these NK cell subsets, we examined athymic nude mice (Foxn1−/−) which lack thymic NK cells but possess liver trNK cells at a somewhat higher percentage when compared to wildtype (WT) controls (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 1B,C showing presence of liver trNK cells in nude mice.

claim: Liver trNK cell numbers are preserved or higher in nude mice.
source: Also, liver trNK cell numbers are preserved or higher in nude mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1D.

claim: Liver trNK cells are present in Gata3fl/fl-Vav-Cre mice.
source: The liver trNK cells from Gata3fl/fl-Vav-Cre mice were present (Figure 1E) whereas CD127+ thymic NK cells were absent in these mice (Figure 1F), as previously shown (Vosshenrich et al., 2006).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 1E and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CD127+ thymic NK cells are absent in Gata3fl/fl-Vav-Cre mice.
source: The liver trNK cells from Gata3fl/fl-Vav-Cre mice were present (Figure 1E) whereas CD127+ thymic NK cells were absent in these mice (Figure 1F), as previously shown (Vosshenrich et al., 2006).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 1F and supported by citation to Vosshenrich et al., 2006.

claim: Liver trNK cells develop independent of the thymus or GATA-3.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the trNK cells from the liver develop independent of the thymus or GATA-3, and can be clearly distinguished from thymic NK cells.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of liver trNK cells in nude and GATA-3 deficient mice.

claim: Liver trNK cells are distinct from liver and splenic cNK cells based on hierarchical clustering of RNA-seq data.
source: Basic hierarchical clustering of the three populations revealed that liver trNK cells are distinct from the liver and splenic cNK cells, which in turn, are more closely related to each other than to liver trNK cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Liver trNK cells display an 'immature' phenotype characterized by CD27+CD11blow expression.
source: Liver trNK cells could be dissimilar from liver and splenic cNK cells perhaps due to their 'immature' phenotype, that is, CD27+CD11blow (Figure 2B) and TRAIL+ (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 2B.

claim: Liver trNK cells express TRAIL.
source: Liver trNK cells could be dissimilar from liver and splenic cNK cells perhaps due to their 'immature' phenotype, that is, CD27+CD11blow (Figure 2B) and TRAIL+ (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 2C.

claim: CD49a+DX5− cells in the liver do not display the gene expression pattern specific to immature CD49a+DX5− NK cells in the bone marrow.
source: When we compared the levels of genes specific to immature CD49a+DX5− NK cell in the BM (Supplementary file 1) to levels of these genes in the other cell subsets, we found that the CD49a+DX5– cells in the liver did not display this cell-type specific pattern (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression comparison shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CD49a−DX5+ subsets in BM, liver and spleen are similar to each other (p=0.01).
source: These relative comparisons to the DX5− subsets showed that the CD49a−DX5+ subsets in BM, liver and spleen were similar to each other (p=0.01).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene set enrichment analysis with statistical significance.

claim: CD49a+DX5− BM NK cells and liver CD49a+DX5− trNK cells are dissimilar (p=0.5).
source: However, the CD49a+DX5− BM NK cells and liver CD49a+DX5− trNK cells were dissimilar (p=0.5) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene set enrichment analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Liver trNK cells represent a separate lineage of NK cells rather than a population of immature NK cells transitioning to mature cNK cells.
source: Taken together with our previous analysis with a much more limited panel of cell surface markers (Peng et al., 2013), these transcriptome data strongly suggest that the trNK cells in the liver are not a population of immature NK cells that are transitioning to mature cNK cells rather they represent a separate lineage of NK cells and indicate the CD49a−DX5+ subsets in BM, liver, and spleen likely represent the same recirculating population of cNK cells.
evidence: Inferred from transcriptome analysis and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Liver trNK cells express Ly49A, C/I, I, F, and G2 at much lower frequencies than cNK cells from both the liver and spleen.
source: The liver trNK cells express Ly49A, C/I, I, F, and G2 at much lower frequencies than cNK cells from both the liver and spleen (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Ly49D and Ly49H activation receptors are not expressed on liver trNK cells.
source: Indeed, some receptors, such as the Ly49D and Ly49H activation receptors, are not expressed on trNK cells.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the receptor expression analysis.

claim: The frequencies of liver trNK cells expressing Ly49E and NKG2A are much higher than liver and splenic cNK cells.
source: However the frequencies of liver trNK cells expressing Ly49E (Ly49EF+ but Ly49F−) and NKG2A are much higher than liver and splenic cNK cells.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the receptor expression analysis.

claim: Liver trNK cells appear larger and more granular by scatter parameters when compared to liver and splenic cNK cells.
source: In addition, the liver trNK cells appear larger and more granular by scatter parameters when compared to the liver and splenic cNK cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry scatter parameters in Figure 3C.

claim: In naïve mice, liver trNK cells express higher levels of CD69, CD44, CD160 and do not express CD62L compared to cNK cells in the liver and spleen.
source: In naïve mice, the liver trNK cells express higher levels of CD69, CD44, CD160 and do not express CD62L as compared to the cNK cells in the liver and spleen, consistent with a more activated state.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis of activation markers.

claim: Liver trNK cells specifically produce easily detectable TNFα and GM-CSF while liver and splenic cNK cells produce these cytokines at much lower levels.
source: The liver trNK cells specifically made easily detectable tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα) and granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) while liver and splenic cNK cells produced these cytokines at much lower levels, if at all (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by cytokine production assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Liver trNK cells make similar amounts of IFNγ when compared to liver and splenic cNK cells.
source: By contrast, the liver trNK cells made similar amounts of interferon-γ (IFNγ) when compared to liver and splenic cNK cells.
evidence: Stated as a finding from cytokine production analysis.

claim: A significant proportion of liver trNK cells are IFNγ+TNFα+ double producers.
source: Interestingly when we analyzed IFNγ and TNFα simultaneously, we found a significant proportion of the liver trNK cells were IFNγ+TNFα+ double producers (Figure 4B,C), a population essentially absent among the cNK cells from the liver and spleen.
evidence: Demonstrated by dual cytokine staining shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Both liver trNK and cNK cells show degranulation as evidenced by CD107a expression in response to YAC-1 targets.
source: Although both trNK and cNK cells showed degranulation, as evidenced by CD107a expression, the degranulating liver trNK cells also produced TNFα that was rarely seen among the responding cNK cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by degranulation assay with YAC-1 targets.

claim: Degranulating liver trNK cells produce TNFα, which is rarely seen among responding cNK cells.
source: Although both trNK and cNK cells showed degranulation, as evidenced by CD107a expression, the degranulating liver trNK cells also produced TNFα that was rarely seen among the responding cNK cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by degranulation assay with YAC-1 targets.

claim: IL-15Rα deficiency results in an absence of liver trNK cells as well as liver and splenic cNK cells.
source: The development of all NK1.1+ CD3− cells was negatively impacted by the IL-15Rα deficiency, resulting in an absence of liver trNK cells as well as liver and splenic cNK cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in IL-15Rα-deficient mice shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Eomes transcripts are expressed at lower levels in liver trNK cells compared to liver and splenic cNK cells.
source: Particularly informative was decreased transcript levels of eomesodermin (Eomes) in the liver trNK cells as compared to liver and splenic cNK cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Liver trNK cells show lower levels of Eomes protein compared to cNK cells.
source: The differences in Eomes transcript levels were verified by flow cytometry which showed lower levels of Eomes protein in liver trNK as compared to cNK cells (Figure 5C), consistent with previous reports (Gordon et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 5C and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There is no relative difference between liver trNK cells and liver and splenic cNK cells in Tbx21 (Tbet) expression at either the transcript or protein level.
source: By contrast, there was no relative difference between liver trNK cells and liver and splenic cNK cells in Tbx21 (Tbet) expression at either the transcript or protein level (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq and flow cytometry data in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Liver trNK cells are present in NFIL3-deficient mice.
source: Surprisingly, in NFIL3-deficient mice, liver trNK cells were present in total cell number (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in NFIL3-deficient mice shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: NFIL3-deficient mice have no cNK cells in the spleen.
source: Conversely, as previously reported, NFIL3-deficient mice had no cNK cells in the spleen (Gascoyne et al., 2009; Kamizono et al., 2009; Kashiwada et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as a finding consistent with previous reports, supported by citations.

claim: NFIL3-deficient mice have no cNK cells in the liver.
source: As well, there were no cNK cells in the liver (Figure 5D,E), consistent with their relationship to splenic cNK cells and raising the percentage of liver trNK cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Liver trNK cells are absent in Tbet-deficient mice in both percentage and total cell number.
source: By contrast, liver trNK cells were absent in Tbet-deficient mice in both percentage and total cell number, when compared to WT controls and in contradistinction to both cNK cell populations (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Tbet-deficient mice shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The requirement for Tbet is consistent with an intrinsic requirement for Tbet in development of TRAIL+ liver NK cells.
source: The requirement for Tbet is consistent with an intrinsic requirement for Tbet in development of TRAIL+ liver NK cells (Gordon et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as consistent with previous findings, supported by citation.

claim: Liver trNK cells are not precursors of cNK cells.
source: Thus, these data demonstrate a unique developmental pathway of liver trNK cells that does not require NFIL3 but depends on Tbx21, indicating that the liver trNK cells are not precursors of cNK cells.
evidence: Inferred from differential transcription factor requirements.

claim: trNK cells from Nfil3−/− mice express markers correlated with activation (higher FSC and SSC, higher levels of CD69 and CD44 and lower levels of CD62L).
source: We found that much like the liver trNK cells from a WT mouse, the trNK cells from Nfil3−/− mice also express markers correlated with activation, that is, higher FSC and SSC, higher levels of CD69 and CD44 and lower levels of CD62L (Figure 5F) and do not express Eomes (Figure 5G).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: trNK cells from Nfil3−/− mice do not express Eomes.
source: We found that much like the liver trNK cells from a WT mouse, the trNK cells from Nfil3−/− mice also express markers correlated with activation, that is, higher FSC and SSC, higher levels of CD69 and CD44 and lower levels of CD62L (Figure 5F) and do not express Eomes (Figure 5G).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Nfil3−/− trNK cells in the liver have an 'immature' phenotype similar to WT trNK cells in that they express CD27 and generally lack CD11b expression on most cells.
source: They have an 'immature' phenotype similar to the WT trNK cells in that they express CD27 and generally lack CD11b expression on most cells (Figure 5H).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Upon stimulation, Nfil3−/− trNK cells in the liver produce both IFNγ+ and TNFα+ simultaneously in a manner comparable to WT trNK cells.
source: Upon stimulation, the Nfil3−/− trNK cells in the liver produce both IFNγ+ and TNFα+ simultaneously in a manner comparable to WT trNK cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: Demonstrated by cytokine production assay shown in Figure 5I.

claim: NFIL3 is not required for normal trNK cells in the liver.
source: Thus, NFIL3 is not required for normal trNK cells in the liver.
evidence: Inferred from the presence and normal phenotype of trNK cells in NFIL3-deficient mice.

claim: Liver trNK cells require different transcription factors than liver and splenic cNK cells.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that liver trNK cells require different transcription factors than liver and splenic cNK cells, providing strong evidence that the liver trNK cells are a distinct lineage from the liver and splenic cNK cells, whereas both cNK cell populations are likely to be developmentally identical.
evidence: Inferred from differential requirements for NFIL3 and Tbet.

claim: Both liver and splenic cNK cell populations are likely to be developmentally identical.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that liver trNK cells require different transcription factors than liver and splenic cNK cells, providing strong evidence that the liver trNK cells are a distinct lineage from the liver and splenic cNK cells, whereas both cNK cell populations are likely to be developmentally identical.
evidence: Inferred from their similar transcription factor requirements.

claim: Large percentages of CD49a+DX5− NK cells are found in the uterus and skin but not in other organs examined.
source: In addition to the liver, we found large percentages of CD49a+DX5− NK cells in the uterus and skin but not in other organs examined (Figure 6A,B), suggesting that CD49a may be a marker of trNK cells in these organs.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis of multiple organs shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: CD49a+ NK cells in the uterus and skin generally lack expression of DX5.
source: The CD49a+ NK cells in the uterus and skin also generally lacked expression of DX5 (Figure 6B) and displayed constitutive expression of CD69, much like the liver trNK cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: CD49a+ NK cells in the uterus and skin display constitutive expression of CD69.
source: The CD49a+ NK cells in the uterus and skin also generally lacked expression of DX5 (Figure 6B) and displayed constitutive expression of CD69, much like the liver trNK cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Host CD49a+ DX5− NK cells in the uterus and skin are primarily found in the indicated host tissue in parabiotic mice.
source: In both the uterus and skin, host CD49a+ DX5− NK cells were primarily found in the indicated host tissue (Figure 6D,F), similar to the CD49a+ DX5− trNK cells in the liver (Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by parabiosis experiments shown in Figure 6D,F and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CD45 allotype-disparate mice reach nearly complete chimerism in the spleen.
source: By contrast, CD45 allotype-disparate mice reached nearly complete chimerism in the spleen (Figure 6E) (Wright et al., 2001; Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by parabiosis experiments shown in Figure 6E and supported by citations.

claim: CD49a−DX5+ NK cells of both allotypes are found in both parabionts, indicating that they are circulating NK cells.
source: Moreover, the CD49a−DX5+ NK cells of both allotypes were found in both parabionts, indicating that they were circulating NK cells, akin to the CD49a−DX5+ cNK cells in the liver (Figure 6D,F).
evidence: Demonstrated by parabiosis experiments shown in Figure 6D,F.

claim: The uterus and skin contain both trNK (CD49a+ DX5−) and circulating cNK (CD49a−DX5+) cells.
source: Thus, the uterus and skin contain both trNK (CD49a+ DX5−) and circulating cNK (CD49a−DX5+) cNK cells, with the trNK cells appearing to dominate the uterine NK cell population.
evidence: Inferred from parabiosis experiments and flow cytometry analysis.

claim: trNK cells appear to dominate the uterine NK cell population.
source: Thus, the uterus and skin contain both trNK (CD49a+ DX5−) and circulating cNK (CD49a−DX5+) cNK cells, with the trNK cells appearing to dominate the uterine NK cell population.
evidence: Inferred from the relative proportions observed in flow cytometry analysis.

claim: Skin trNK cells do not express Eomes.
source: The skin trNK cells do not express Eomes and are absent in IL-15Rα-deficient mice (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Skin trNK cells are absent in IL-15Rα-deficient mice.
source: The skin trNK cells do not express Eomes and are absent in IL-15Rα-deficient mice (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: trNK cells in the uterus and skin produce more IL-2 than cNK cells in the liver and spleen.
source: Furthermore the trNK cells in the uterus and skin produce more IL-2 than cNK cells in the liver and spleen (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated by intracellular cytokine staining shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Tissue-resident CD49a+DX5− cells in the liver, uterus and skin do not express CD127.
source: First, we found no detectable CD127 expression on uterine and skin trNK cells when compared to the CD127 expression on the thymic NK cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Uterine and skin trNK cells are present in Foxn1−/− (athymic) mice.
source: Second, we found uterine and skin trNK cells are present in Foxn1−/−(athymic) mice (Figure 7E), indicating that they develop independent of a thymus, unlike thymic NK cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in athymic mice shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Uterine and skin trNK cells develop independent of a thymus.
source: Second, we found uterine and skin trNK cells are present in Foxn1−/−(athymic) mice (Figure 7E), indicating that they develop independent of a thymus, unlike thymic NK cells.
evidence: Inferred from their presence in athymic mice.

claim: trNK cells are present in the liver, uterus and skin of NFIL3-deficient mice.
source: Strikingly, trNK cells were present in the liver, uterus and skin of NFIL3-deficient mice (Figure 8A,B), indicating that these trNK cells represent a distinct lineage from cNK cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in NFIL3-deficient mice shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Circulating CD49a−DX5+ NK cells are absent in the liver, uterus and skin of NFIL3-deficient mice.
source: Moreover, the circulating CD49a−DX5+ NK cells were absent in these tissues, indicating that these CD49a−DX5+ NK cells are related to the cNK cells in the liver and spleen.
evidence: Stated as a finding from analysis of NFIL3-deficient mice.

claim: CD49a−DX5+ NK cells are related to the cNK cells in the liver and spleen.
source: Moreover, the circulating CD49a−DX5+ NK cells were absent in these tissues, indicating that these CD49a−DX5+ NK cells are related to the cNK cells in the liver and spleen.
evidence: Inferred from their absence in NFIL3-deficient mice.

claim: trNK cells are absent in skin of Tbet-deficient mice.
source: In Tbet-deficient mice, the trNK cells were absent in skin (Figure 8A,B) akin to liver trNK cells (Figure 5D,E), implying a developmental link between the trNK cells in the liver and skin.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Tbet-deficient mice shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: There is a developmental link between the trNK cells in the liver and skin.
source: In Tbet-deficient mice, the trNK cells were absent in skin (Figure 8A,B) akin to liver trNK cells (Figure 5D,E), implying a developmental link between the trNK cells in the liver and skin.
evidence: Inferred from their shared requirement for Tbet.

claim: Uterine trNK cells are present in Tbet-deficient mice.
source: Interestingly, however, the uterine trNK cells were still present in Tbet-deficient mice (Figure 8A,B), strongly suggesting that uterine trNK cells represent yet another NK cell lineage.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Tbet-deficient mice shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Uterine trNK cells represent yet another NK cell lineage distinct from liver and skin trNK cells.
source: Interestingly, however, the uterine trNK cells were still present in Tbet-deficient mice (Figure 8A,B), strongly suggesting that uterine trNK cells represent yet another NK cell lineage.
evidence: Inferred from their presence in Tbet-deficient mice while liver and skin trNK cells are absent.

claim: There are at least four lineages of NK cells: cNK cells circulating in spleen, blood and other organs, thymic, and two trNK cell lineages—liver (and skin), and uterine.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that there are at least four lineages of NK cells: cNK cells circulating in spleen, blood and other organs, thymic, and two trNK cell lineages—liver (and skin), and uterine.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive analysis of transcription factor requirements and tissue distribution.

claim: trNK cells do not require the putative NK cell specification factor, NFIL3.
source: Most importantly, trNK cells do not require the putative NK cell specification factor, NFIL3 (Di Santo, 2009; Gascoyne et al., 2009; Kamizono et al., 2009; Kashiwada et al., 2010), indicating that they belong to a different cell lineage.
evidence: Demonstrated by presence of trNK cells in NFIL3-deficient mice and supported by citations.

claim: trNK cells belong to a different cell lineage from cNK cells.
source: Most importantly, trNK cells do not require the putative NK cell specification factor, NFIL3 (Di Santo, 2009; Gascoyne et al., 2009; Kamizono et al., 2009; Kashiwada et al., 2010), indicating that they belong to a different cell lineage.
evidence: Inferred from differential NFIL3 requirement.

claim: In the liver, skin, and uterus, trNK cells differentially express CD49a.
source: In the liver, skin, and uterus, they differentially express CD49a, though it is possible that trNK cells in other organs preferentially express another marker.
evidence: Stated as a finding from flow cytometry analysis.

claim: trNK cells lack DX5 expression which is generally expressed as a late maturation marker on most cNK cells.
source: Concomitantly, they lack DX5 expression which is generally expressed as a late maturation marker on most cNK cells (Kim et al., 2002; Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as a finding and supported by citations.

claim: trNK cells from unmanipulated mice display markers associated with cNK cell activation, such as CD69.
source: Interestingly, trNK cells from unmanipulated mice display markers associated with cNK cell activation, such as CD69, in contrast to cNK cells which do not express CD69 until activated (Karlhofer and Yokoyama, 1991; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated as a finding and supported by citations.

claim: cNK cells do not express CD69 until activated.
source: Interestingly, trNK cells from unmanipulated mice display markers associated with cNK cell activation, such as CD69, in contrast to cNK cells which do not express CD69 until activated (Karlhofer and Yokoyama, 1991; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: trNK cells express a different repertoire of Ly49 receptors compared to cNK cells.
source: The trNK cells also express a different repertoire of Ly49 receptors, suggesting that they may be tolerant to self by using mechanisms that do not strictly employ MHC class I-dependent licensing by Ly49 receptors, as has been shown for cNK cells in the spleen (Kim et al., 2005; Elliott and Yokoyama, 2011).
evidence: Stated as a finding and supported by citations.

claim: trNK cells may be tolerant to self by using mechanisms that do not strictly employ MHC class I-dependent licensing by Ly49 receptors.
source: The trNK cells also express a different repertoire of Ly49 receptors, suggesting that they may be tolerant to self by using mechanisms that do not strictly employ MHC class I-dependent licensing by Ly49 receptors, as has been shown for cNK cells in the spleen (Kim et al., 2005; Elliott and Yokoyama, 2011).
evidence: Speculated based on differential Ly49 receptor expression.

claim: trNK cells efficiently produce TNFα and GM-CSF which may contribute to inflammatory conditions in a manner distinct from cNK cells which predominantly produce IFNγ.
source: The trNK cells efficiently produce other cytokines, particularly TNFα and GM-CSF which may contribute to inflammatory conditions in a manner distinct from cNK cells which predominantly produce IFNγ.
evidence: Stated as a finding with speculation about functional implications.

claim: TNFα production in trNK cells occurs following stimulation by target cells and also occurs in trNK cells producing IFNγ.
source: TNFα production occurs following stimulation by target cells and also occurs in trNK cells producing IFNγ.
evidence: Stated as a finding from stimulation experiments.

claim: trNK cells utilize a separate set of transcription factors which may endow trNK cells with other unique functions, in addition to lineage commitment.
source: Finally, trNK cells utilize a separate set of transcription factors which may endow trNK cells with other unique functions, in addition to lineage commitment.
evidence: Stated as a finding with speculation about functional implications.

claim: Due to their tissue localization and distinctive features, trNK cells most likely play important roles in innate defense in ways that should be distinguishable from cNK cells.
source: As such, due to their tissue localization and these distinctive features, trNK cells most likely play important roles in innate defense in ways that should be distinguishable from cNK cells.
evidence: Speculated based on their distinctive characteristics.

claim: Liver and skin trNK cells are phenotypically similar.
source: Among the various NK cell lineages, the liver and skin trNK cells appear to be highly related. They are phenotypically similar and both are absent in Tbet-deficient mice.
evidence: Stated as a finding from phenotypic analysis.

claim: Liver and skin trNK cells are more related to each other than to other NK cell lineages, including cNK cells.
source: Although it remains to be formally shown that a common precursor can give rise to liver and skin trNK cells but not other NK cell lineages, these data indicate that they are more related to each other than to other NK cell lineages, including cNK cells.
evidence: Inferred from their shared phenotypic and transcription factor characteristics.

claim: uNK cells appear distinct from the liver and skin trNK cells because they are Tbet-independent.
source: uNK cells appear distinct from the liver and skin trNK cells because they are Tbet-independent, even though all are NFIL3-independent.
evidence: Stated as a finding from analysis of Tbet-deficient mice.

claim: uNK cells express Eomes at high levels.
source: Perhaps this is due to concomitant expression of Eomes at high levels in uNK cells (Tayade et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated as a possibility supported by citation.

claim: Both trNK and cNK cells do not express high levels of CD127 that is characteristic of thymic NK cells.
source: The liver, skin, and uterine trNK cell lineages can be distinguished from thymic NK cells in several ways. Both trNK (as shown here) and cNK cells do not express high levels of CD127 that is characteristic of thymic NK cells (Vosshenrich et al., 2006; Yadi et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated as a finding and supported by citations.

claim: Thymic NK cells are absent in nude mice and in mice lacking GATA-3 which possess cNK cells.
source: Moreover, thymic NK cells are absent in nude mice and in mice lacking GATA-3 which possess cNK cells, as recapitulated here.
evidence: Stated as a finding from analysis of nude and GATA-3 deficient mice.

claim: cNK, uterine and liver trNK cells can respond to YAC-1 targets by degranulation and killing.
source: As shown here and previously published, cNK, uterine and liver trNK cells can respond to YAC-1 targets by degranulation and killing (Kiessling et al., 1975; Linnemeyer and Pollack, 1991; Peng et al., 2013), though this needs to be further detailed for the skin trNK cells described here.
evidence: Stated as a finding and supported by citations.

claim: cNK cells require IL-15 or IL-15Rα.
source: Moreover, cNK cells require IL-15 or IL-15Rα (Lodolce et al., 1998; Kennedy et al., 2000) and here we showed that IL-15Rα-deficient mice have no cNK or trNK cells, such that no NK1.1+ CD3− cells were identifiable in spleen, liver, and skin of the knockout mice.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IL-15Rα-deficient mice have no cNK or trNK cells, such that no NK1.1+ CD3− cells are identifiable in spleen, liver, and skin.
source: Moreover, cNK cells require IL-15 or IL-15Rα (Lodolce et al., 1998; Kennedy et al., 2000) and here we showed that IL-15Rα-deficient mice have no cNK or trNK cells, such that no NK1.1+ CD3− cells were identifiable in spleen, liver, and skin of the knockout mice.
evidence: Stated as a finding from analysis of IL-15Rα-deficient mice.

claim: IL-15-deficient mice lack NK1.1+ CD3− cells in the uterus.
source: Similarly, IL-15-deficient mice lack NK1.1+ CD3− cells in the uterus (Ashkar et al., 2003; Barber and Pollard, 2003), indicating that trNK cells in the uterus as well as liver and skin are IL-15Rα-dependent.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: trNK cells in the uterus as well as liver and skin are IL-15Rα-dependent.
source: Similarly, IL-15-deficient mice lack NK1.1+ CD3− cells in the uterus (Ashkar et al., 2003; Barber and Pollard, 2003), indicating that trNK cells in the uterus as well as liver and skin are IL-15Rα-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of these cells in IL-15 and IL-15Rα-deficient mice.

claim: Current data support the intimate relationship between trNK and cNK cells, particularly cytotoxic potential and IL-15-dependence.
source: While more detailed analysis of the progenitors for NK cells will be required to establish the precise lineage relationship of trNK and cNK cells to each other, current data, particularly cytotoxic potential and IL-15-dependence, support their intimate relationship, despite differences in transcription factor requirements.
evidence: Inferred from shared functional characteristics despite different transcription factor requirements.

claim: cNK cells belong to the group 1 ILCs, due to their shared production of IFNγ.
source: cNK cells are now classified as belonging to the group 1 ILCs, due to their shared production of IFNγ.
evidence: Stated as current classification knowledge.

claim: cNK cells can be distinguished from other group 1 ILCs by their cytotoxic capacities, dependence on IL-15, and general lack of IL7Rα expression.
source: cNK cells can be distinguished from other group 1 ILCs by their cytotoxic capacities, dependence on IL-15, and general lack of IL7Rα expression, features shared between cNK and liver, skin, and uterine trNK cells.
evidence: Stated as distinguishing characteristics.

claim: Features that distinguish cNK cells from other group 1 ILCs are shared between cNK and liver, skin, and uterine trNK cells.
source: cNK cells can be distinguished from other group 1 ILCs by their cytotoxic capacities, dependence on IL-15, and general lack of IL7Rα expression, features shared between cNK and liver, skin, and uterine trNK cells.
evidence: Stated as a finding from comparative analysis.

claim: A new IFNγ-producing ILC1 cell was identified which demonstrated dependence on NFIL3, Tbx21, and IL-15 but not IL-15Rα.
source: Recently, a new IFNγ-producing ILC1 cell was identified which demonstrated dependence on NFIL3, Tbx21, and IL-15 but not IL-15Rα (Fuchs et al., 2013), unlike the trNK cells described here.
evidence: Stated as recent finding supported by citation.

claim: The new IFNγ-producing ILC1 cell is unlike the trNK cells described in this study.
source: Recently, a new IFNγ-producing ILC1 cell was identified which demonstrated dependence on NFIL3, Tbx21, and IL-15 but not IL-15Rα (Fuchs et al., 2013), unlike the trNK cells described here.
evidence: Stated as a distinction based on different requirements.

claim: Liver (skin) and uterine trNK cells are more related to cNK cells than ILCs.
source: Finally, while the relationship of thymic NK cells expressing CD127 to ILCs which also express CD127 may need further refinement, current knowledge suggest that the liver (skin) and uterine trNK cells are more related to cNK cells than ILCs.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on current knowledge.

claim: Markers previously thought to be exclusively expressed on NK cells, such as NKp46, are expressed on ILCs that can be distinguished from classical NK cells.
source: Already, it has been noted that markers previously thought to be exclusively expressed on NK cells, such as NKp46, are expressed on ILCs that now can be distinguished from classical NK cells (Walzer et al., 2007; Cella et al., 2009; Spits et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ILCs display apparent plasticity with potential interconversion between ILC groups.
source: A further confounding issue is the apparent plasticity of ILCs with potential interconversion between ILC groups (Cella et al., 2010; Vonarbourg et al., 2010), indicating the increasing complexities of definitively identifying ILC types and potentially distinguishing ILCs from other immune cells.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that trNK cells may be more closely related to certain ILCs than currently appreciated.
source: Thus, it is possible that trNK cells may be more closely related to certain ILCs than currently appreciated.
evidence: Stated as speculation about potential relationships.

claim: ILC2s in the skin regulate cutaneous inflammation but are unaffected by IL15-deficiency.
source: ILC2s in the skin have been reported to regulate cutaneous inflammation but they are unaffected by IL15-deficiency (Roediger et al., 2013), unlike trNK cells as shown here.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ILC2s in the skin are unlike trNK cells because they are unaffected by IL15-deficiency.
source: ILC2s in the skin have been reported to regulate cutaneous inflammation but they are unaffected by IL15-deficiency (Roediger et al., 2013), unlike trNK cells as shown here.
evidence: Stated as a distinction based on IL-15 requirement.

claim: In the uterus, a phenotypically related but distinct population of cells express the transcription factor RORC and produce IL-22, suggesting they may be ILC3s rather than NK cells.
source: In the uterus, immature NK cells have been described as well as a phenotypically related but distinct population of cells that express the transcription factor RORC and produce IL-22, suggesting that they may be ILC3s rather than NK cells (Crellin et al., 2010; Male et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NKT cells share several characteristics with trNK cells in the liver.
source: Of these, NKT cells are of special interest because they share several characteristics with trNK cells in the liver.
evidence: Stated as an observation about shared characteristics.

claim: A large number of NKT cells reside in the liver, though they can be found in other tissues.
source: While they are now known to recognize glycolipids presented by CD1 molecules, a large number of NKT cells also reside in the liver, though they can be found in other tissues.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: In the liver, NKT cells crawl within the sinusoidal space by patrolling sinusoidal endothelial cells.
source: In the liver, NKT cells crawl within the sinusoidal space by patrolling sinusoidal endothelial cells (Geissmann et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Pit cells are found in the sinusoidal space usually adjacent to sinusoidal endothelial cells.
source: Pit cells are found in the sinusoidal space usually adjacent to sinusoidal endothelial cells.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: It seems likely that liver trNK cells are related to, if not equivalent to, pit cells.
source: Although liver trNK cells have not been formally examined vis-à-vis pit cells, it seems likely that they are related, if not equivalent.
evidence: Stated as speculation based on anatomical similarities.

claim: Tissue-resident memory T cells had been previously activated by antigen-stimulation and differentiated into effector cells that then reside in non-lymphoid tissues.
source: The trNK cell populations also are potentially related to tissue-resident memory T cells which had been previously activated by antigen-stimulation and differentiated into effector cells that then reside in non-lymphoid tissues (Sheridan and Lefrancois, 2011; Gebhardt et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: trNK cells appear to have an activated phenotype with expression of CD69 and other activation markers as well as other phenotypic changes.
source: Our studies indicate that trNK cells appear to have an activated phenotype with expression of CD69 and other activation markers as well as other phenotypic changes.
evidence: Stated as a finding from phenotypic analysis.

claim: It is not yet clear if trNK cells differentiate from a circulating precursor that then differentiates into a cell taking up tissue residency, akin to tissue-resident memory T cells.
source: However, it is not yet clear if trNK cells differentiate from a circulating precursor that then differentiates into a cell taking up tissue residency, akin to tissue-resident memory T cells (Masopust et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as an unresolved question.

claim: The transcription factor requirements make it unlikely that a putative circulating precursor of trNK cells is an NK cell that had previously differentiated into a cNK cell.
source: Our studies do not rule out this possibility although the transcription factor requirements make it unlikely that a putative circulating precursor is an NK cell that had previously differentiated into a cNK cell.
evidence: Inferred from differential transcription factor requirements.

claim: Ly49E was first noted to be almost exclusively expressed on fetal NK cells.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that Ly49E was first noted to be almost exclusively expressed on fetal NK cells (Toomey et al., 1998).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Liver trNK cells in adult mice selectively express Ly49E.
source: However, recent findings (Filtjens et al., 2013) and those reported here indicate that liver trNK cells in adult mice also selectively express Ly49E, raising the possibility that Ly49E+ NK cells in the fetus reflect trNK cells already present in the embryonic liver, at a time when cNK cells are poorly developed (Bukowski et al., 1985; Dorfman and Raulet, 1998).
evidence: Stated as a finding and supported by citations.

claim: Ly49E+ NK cells in the fetus may reflect trNK cells already present in the embryonic liver.
source: However, recent findings (Filtjens et al., 2013) and those reported here indicate that liver trNK cells in adult mice also selectively express Ly49E, raising the possibility that Ly49E+ NK cells in the fetus reflect trNK cells already present in the embryonic liver, at a time when cNK cells are poorly developed (Bukowski et al., 1985; Dorfman and Raulet, 1998).
evidence: Stated as speculation based on Ly49E expression patterns.

claim: Precursors of liver trNK cells are present in the adult liver.
source: Consistent with this possibility, we recently showed that precursors of liver trNK cells are present in the adult liver (Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous work supported by citation.

claim: Adult BM hematopoietic stem cells do not fully reconstitute the liver trNK cell population in irradiated mice.
source: Moreover, adult BM hematopoietic stem cells do not fully reconstitute the liver trNK cell population in irradiated mice.
evidence: Stated as a finding.

claim: Precursors of trNK cells, like γδT cells and certain tissue macrophages, may seed tissues early in life.
source: Thus, precursors of trNK cells, like γδT cells and certain tissue macrophages (Havran and Allison, 1990; Schulz et al., 2012), may seed tissues early in life, a topic that will require further evaluation.
evidence: Stated as speculation supported by citations to similar cell types.

claim: NK cells require IL-15 and its cognate receptor, IL-15R, for development.
source: NK cells require IL-15 and its cognate receptor, IL-15R, for development (Cao et al., 1995; DiSanto et al., 1995; Suzuki et al., 1997; Lodolce et al., 1998; Kennedy et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In knockout mice lacking IL-15 or any chain of the trimeric IL-15R (α, β, γ), splenic NK cells are absent.
source: In knockout mice lacking IL-15 or any chain of the trimeric IL-15R (α, β, γ), splenic NK cells are absent.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: The development of splenic NK cells is thought to occur largely if not exclusively in the bone marrow.
source: The development of splenic NK cells is thought to occur largely if not exclusively in the bone marrow (BM) where cells committed to the NK cell lineage undergo a series of putative developmental stages, characterized by acquisition and loss of various surface markers, including cytokine receptors, NK cell receptors, and integrins (Kim et al., 2002; Yokoyama et al., 2004; Di Santo, 2006).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mature splenic NK cells can be distinguished by differential expression of CD11b and CD27.
source: Out in the periphery, mature splenic NK cells can be further distinguished by differential expression of CD11b and CD27 (Kim et al., 2002; Hayakawa and Smyth, 2006).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NFIL3 (E4BP4) is described as the NK cell-specification factor.
source: NK cells require certain transcription factors for development (Hesslein and Lanier, 2011), in particular NFIL3 (E4BP4), described as the NK cell-specification factor (Di Santo, 2009).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mice lacking NFIL3 have essentially no splenic NK cells.
source: Mice lacking NFIL3 have essentially no splenic NK cells though other organs were not thoroughly examined (Gascoyne et al., 2009; Kamizono et al., 2009; Kashiwada et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of Tbet, splenic NK cells display an immature phenotype.
source: In the absence of Tbet, splenic NK cells display an immature phenotype, and a subpopulation of NK cells in the liver is absent, consistent with overlapping and cooperative roles of Tbet and Eomes in NK cell development.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: A subpopulation of NK cells in the liver is absent in Tbet-deficient mice.
source: In the absence of Tbet, splenic NK cells display an immature phenotype, and a subpopulation of NK cells in the liver is absent, consistent with overlapping and cooperative roles of Tbet and Eomes in NK cell development.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: Thymic NK cells are cytotoxic and require IL-15.
source: Like the conventional NK (cNK) cells in the spleen, thymic NK cells are cytotoxic and require IL-15 but they differ from cNK cells by their characteristic expression of CD127 (IL-7 receptor α) and requirement for a thymus where they can arise from early thymocyte precursors (Vosshenrich et al., 2006; Ribeiro et al., 2010; Vargas et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Thymic NK cells differ from cNK cells by their characteristic expression of CD127 (IL-7 receptor α) and requirement for a thymus.
source: Like the conventional NK (cNK) cells in the spleen, thymic NK cells are cytotoxic and require IL-15 but they differ from cNK cells by their characteristic expression of CD127 (IL-7 receptor α) and requirement for a thymus where they can arise from early thymocyte precursors (Vosshenrich et al., 2006; Ribeiro et al., 2010; Vargas et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Thymic NK cells uniquely require the transcription factor GATA-3 for development.
source: Furthermore, thymic NK cells uniquely require the transcription factor GATA-3 for development (Vosshenrich et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NK cells are normally present in the non-pregnant uterus.
source: NK cells are normally present in the non-pregnant uterus (Parr et al., 1991; Yadi et al., 2008; Mallidi et al., 2009) but have been mostly studied after they expand at the site of embryo implantation during pregnancy (Moffett and Loke, 2006; Hatta et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: uNK cells require IL-15 for development.
source: Like cNK cells, uterine NK (uNK) cells require IL-15 for development (Ashkar et al., 2003).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: uNK cells are cytotoxic as they express perforin and granzymes, and they produce IFNγ.
source: In addition, they are cytotoxic as they express perforin and granzymes, and they produce IFNγ (Parr et al., 1990; Ashkar et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: uNK cells appear relatively normal in Tbet-deficient mice.
source: Interestingly, however, uNK cells appear relatively normal in Tbet-deficient mice (Tayade et al., 2005) and recent studies suggest that a subset of uNK cells can be distinguished from cNK cells (Yadi et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A subset of uNK cells can be distinguished from cNK cells.
source: Interestingly, however, uNK cells appear relatively normal in Tbet-deficient mice (Tayade et al., 2005) and recent studies suggest that a subset of uNK cells can be distinguished from cNK cells (Yadi et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the liver, there are two populations of NK cells, distinguished by mutually exclusive expression of CD49a and DX5.
source: In the liver, we recently showed that there are two populations of NK cells, distinguished by mutually exclusive expression of CD49a and DX5 (Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous work supported by citation.

claim: CD49a−DX5+ liver NK cells are very similar to splenic cNK cells.
source: Phenotypically, CD49a−DX5+ are very similar to splenic cNK cells whereas CD49a+ DX5– are unlike splenic cNK cells.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: CD49a+ DX5− liver NK cells are unlike splenic cNK cells.
source: Phenotypically, CD49a−DX5+ are very similar to splenic cNK cells whereas CD49a+ DX5– are unlike splenic cNK cells.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: In parabiotic mice, the host liver contains CD49a+ DX5− NK cells of host origin.
source: In parabiotic mice, the host liver contains CD49a+ DX5− NK cells of host origin and circulating CD49a−DX5+ NK cells derived from both host and the other parabiont, indicating that the CD49a+ DX5− cells are tissue-resident NK (trNK) cells whereas the CD49a−DX5+ cells are cNK cells.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: In parabiotic mice, the host liver contains circulating CD49a−DX5+ NK cells derived from both host and the other parabiont.
source: In parabiotic mice, the host liver contains CD49a+ DX5− NK cells of host origin and circulating CD49a−DX5+ NK cells derived from both host and the other parabiont, indicating that the CD49a+ DX5− cells are tissue-resident NK (trNK) cells whereas the CD49a−DX5+ cells are cNK cells.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: CD49a+ DX5− cells in the liver are tissue-resident NK (trNK) cells.
source: In parabiotic mice, the host liver contains CD49a+ DX5− NK cells of host origin and circulating CD49a−DX5+ NK cells derived from both host and the other parabiont, indicating that the CD49a+ DX5− cells are tissue-resident NK (trNK) cells whereas the CD49a−DX5+ cells are cNK cells.
evidence: Inferred from parabiosis experiments in previous work.

claim: CD49a−DX5+ cells in the liver are cNK cells.
source: In parabiotic mice, the host liver contains CD49a+ DX5− NK cells of host origin and circulating CD49a−DX5+ NK cells derived from both host and the other parabiont, indicating that the CD49a+ DX5− cells are tissue-resident NK (trNK) cells whereas the CD49a−DX5+ cells are cNK cells.
evidence: Inferred from parabiosis experiments in previous work.

claim: Liver trNK cells appear similar to immature cNK cells because they express similar markers (NK1.1, NKp46) but low levels of CD11b, are DX5−, and display high levels of TRAIL.
source: The trNK cells appear similar to immature cNK cells because they express similar markers (NK1.1, NKp46) but low levels of CD11b, are DX5−, and display high levels of TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) (Kim et al., 2002; Di Santo , 2006; Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as a finding supported by citations.

claim: Liver trNK cells appear to be distinct from immature BM cNK cells because they are cytotoxic and express CD49a.
source: However, the liver trNK cells appear to be distinct from immature BM cNK cells because they are cytotoxic and express CD49a.
evidence: Stated as a finding.

claim: There is a complete absence of TRAIL+ NK cells in the livers of Tbet-deficient mice.
source: Consistent with this possible developmental intermediate stage, there is a complete absence of TRAIL+ NK cells in the livers of Tbet-deficient mice (Gordon et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge supported by citation.
